planting.note: Break off a mature joint with tongs in spring, let the cut end callus for one to two weeks in a dry shaded spot, then set it a few inches into fast-draining soil and withhold water until roots form.

directions: Break off a mature joint (segment) with tongs in spring, let the cut end callus for one to two weeks in a dry shaded spot, then set it a few inches into fast-draining soil and withhold water until roots form. This Sonoran Desert native forms a small silvery-spined tree with pendulous chains of fruit that persist year-round, making it a dramatic accent or barrier planting. Handle with heavy gloves and long tools, since the barbed joints detach at the slightest touch and are notoriously difficult to remove from skin or fabric. Give it full sun and a spot away from foot traffic and pets.

planting.note: Take pencil-thin stem cuttings in spring, cure the cut ends for a week or more, then plant shallowly in gritty, well-drained soil and hold off watering until roots establish.

directions: Take pencil-thin stem cuttings in spring, cure the cut ends for a week or more, then plant shallowly in gritty, well-drained soil and hold off watering until roots establish. This slender, sparsely spined cholla often hides beneath nurse shrubs and becomes most visible in winter when it is studded with bright red, cherry-like fruit that can persist for months. It tolerates more cold than most chollas and works well tucked into rock gardens or native hedgerows where its winter color stands out against gray desert foliage.

planting.note: Root calloused stem segments in spring in sharply draining cactus mix, watering only lightly until new growth confirms establishment.

directions: Root calloused stem segments in spring in sharply draining cactus mix, watering only lightly until new growth confirms establishment. Buckhorn cholla branches into an open, antler-like silhouette with tan to golden spines and produces bronze-orange or yellow flowers in late spring followed by spiny fruit. It is a structural focal point for desert landscapes and mixes well with palo verde or creosote as companion plantings. Keep it well back from paths, since the spiny joints detach easily and are painful to remove.

planting.note: Sow surface-scattered seed on gritty, sterile cactus mix indoors in late winter, keep barely moist and warm until seedlings appear, then transplant outdoors after the danger of frost has passed.

directions: Sow surface-scattered seed on gritty, sterile cactus mix indoors in late winter, keep barely moist and warm until seedlings appear, then transplant outdoors after the danger of frost has passed. Named for its tightly combed, colorful spines that lie flat against the ribs, this low clustering cactus produces large magenta to pink funnel-shaped flowers in late spring. It is a favorite for raised rock gardens and containers where its striking spine patterns can be viewed up close. Protect it from winter wet, which is the most common cause of rot in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter on sterile, mineral-rich cactus mix, then harden off and transplant into the garden once nights stay above freezing.

directions: Start seed indoors in late winter on sterile, mineral-rich cactus mix, then harden off and transplant into the garden once nights stay above freezing. Native to higher-elevation grasslands and woodlands of the Southwest, this species tolerates more cold than many hedgehog cacti and rewards growers with large, brilliant pink-purple blooms each spring. It slowly clusters into small mounds, making it well suited to xeric rock gardens at higher elevations. Excellent drainage is essential, since this species is more susceptible to rot than to cold injury.
